ta-l1d21q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 21. Having shown the persons' equality using expressions with exclusive words attached to personal terms ('the Father alone has as much power as all three'), Lombard asks how exclusive words can be joined to divine names. He asks first whether an exclusive word can be joined to a personal subject with a personal predicate, and then whether it can be joined to a personal name when an essential name is predicated of it ('the Father alone is God'). Such locutions are not to be granted simply, though in some sense they can be, without absurdity, since according to Augustine saying something of the Father alone does not exclude the Son or the Spirit. The exclusive word cannot be added on the side of the predicate either ('the Father is the only God'), against some, though 'the Trinity is the only God' can be said. Thomas announces two inquiries: whether an exclusive word can be added on the side of the subject, and whether on the side of the predicate. The first has two articles: adding it to an essential subject term with an essential or personal predicate, and adding it to a personal term with an essential predicate.
claims: 'The Father alone is God' is not to be granted simply but can be in some sense.
'The Trinity is the only God' is true, though 'the Father is the only God' is not.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e148.summary: First argument that 'God alone is God' is false. Every adjective places its content on its noun, and 'alone' (solus) is an adjective, so 'God alone' implies solitude in God. But according to Hilary, God is to be confessed neither as solitary nor as diverse.
claims: Solus as adjective implies solitude.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e154.summary: Second argument. 'God' has the nature of a common term, so that what is said of God is said of all the persons ('God creates') or of some ('God begets'), and one can descend under it to a person. If 'God alone is God' were true, one of 'the Father alone is God', 'the Son alone is God', 'the Spirit alone is God' would be true, but all are false.
claims: One can descend from 'Deus' to the persons.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e157.summary: Third argument. According to the Philosopher, 'alone' means 'not with another', and God, especially after creation, is never not with another, since he brought things into participation of his being.
claims: Solum means non cum alio.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e160.summary: Sed contra. What is proper belongs to one alone, and divine being or omnipotence is proper to God, so God alone is God or omnipotent.
claims: What is proper belongs to one alone.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e169.summary: Further question about 'God alone is Father', which seems false: what is found in another cannot be in someone alone, and paternity is found not only in God but in humans and in some way in angels (Dionysius).
claims: Paternity is found in creatures too.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e172.summary: Sed contra. If something common is predicated exclusively of a subject, so is something proper predicated of it: if only body is coloured, only body is white, supposing white is predicated of body. 'God' is like a common term relative to the three persons (Damascene), so if God alone is God and God is Father, God alone is Father.
claims: Exclusive predication of the common carries to the proper.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e181.summary: Thomas's answer to the first sub-question. According to the Philosopher, 'alone' means 'not with another', removing companionship. 'Solus' can remove companionship simply or with respect to something. It removes it simply when it removes association with another of the same nature and condition, as a man is alone in a house though many animals are there, or a religious walks alone without a companion of his order; then 'solus' means solitary and is a categorematic word implying solitude in the subject, like any adjective, and in this sense it cannot be used in God, since each person always has the companionship of another connatural person. If it excludes companionship with respect to something determinate, it is a syncategorematic word implying an order of one to another by its implicit negation rather than a form. In this sense 'God alone creates' is twofold. It can remove companionship from the form of the subject, with an implied 'who is', meaning 'God, who is God such that no other is God, creates', which is true. Or it can remove companionship in sharing the predicate, meaning 'no one other than God creates', which is also true. The same holds of 'the Father alone is Father' and 'the Father alone begets': all such are false in the first sense and true in the other two.
claims: 'Solus' taken categorematically implies solitude and cannot be used of God.
Taken syncategorematically, it excludes others either from the subject's form or from the predicate, and in these senses 'God alone creates' is true.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e184.summary: The reply to the first argument follows: it proceeds on the first, categorematic sense.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the second argument. As the logicians say, an exclusive word immobilizes the term it is joined to by its implicit negation, so 'only man is rational, therefore only Socrates' does not follow, since not everything other than Socrates is other than man. The implicit negation extends to more when joined to a proper than to a common term. Descent is possible on the side of the affirmation, though: 'God alone is God' has two exponents, the affirmative 'God is God' and the negative 'what is other than God is not God'. Under the affirmative one can descend ('the Father is God'), but not under the negative ('what is other than the Father is not God').
claims: Exclusive words immobilize their term; descent is valid only under the affirmative exponent.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Solus' removes companionship. Although, with creatures existing, companionship in being cannot be removed from God, it can be removed as to his proper operation, creation, and as to his proper nature. So according to Hilary, with the distinction of persons removed, God would be called solitary even with creatures existing: though 'God alone is' would not be true, 'God is alone', i.e. solitary, would be.
claims: God is alone in his proper operation and nature, though not in being, given creatures.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e194.summary: Concedes the sed contra, which proceeds on the third sense.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e204.summary: Thomas's answer to the second sub-question. 'God alone is Father' is judged three ways. If 'alone' implies solitude in God, it is false. If it excludes others from the subject's form, it is true: 'God, other than whom there is no other, is Father'. If it removes companionship in sharing the predicate, it is twofold. If 'Father' signifies only the property of paternity, the predicate taken formally, it is false, since paternity is in humans too. If it signifies the subsistent person distinguished by paternity, it is true, and the arguments prove and disprove it accordingly. Still, paternity is not of the same character univocally in God and creatures, though it is analogically, which involves both identity and diversity of character. So even taking the predicate formally, 'God alone is Father' can be true in a way, as in 'no one is good but God alone' (Luke 18:19).
claims: 'God alone is Father' is true by exclusion from the subject's form, or of the subsistent person; false of paternity taken formally and univocally.
Paternity is said of God and creatures analogically.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e220.summary: First argument that 'the Father alone is God' or 'the Son alone is God' is true. Being most high belongs to the three persons as being God does, and of the Son it is said 'you alone are the Most High'.
claims: 'Tu solus altissimus' is said of the Son.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e226.summary: Second argument. 'The Father alone is God' has two exponents: an indefinite or singular one, converted like a particular affirmative ('the Father is God'), and a universal negative ('nothing other than the Father is God'), both converting simply. In some sense 'God alone is Father' is true, so by simple conversion 'the Father alone is God' is true.
claims: Exponents convert simply.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e229.summary: Third argument. 'The Father alone is God' would be false only because the exclusive word excludes the other persons from the predicate, but it does not exclude the Son and Spirit. Augustine says that even if these things were said of the Father alone, the Son and Spirit would not be excluded, because they are one. Also, the Son's union with the Father is greater than a part's with its whole, and an exclusive word joined to a whole does not exclude its part ('only Socrates is white' does not imply his foot is not white).
claims: Augustine: saying something of the Father alone does not exclude Son and Spirit.
An exclusive word does not exclude a part from its whole.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e236.summary: Fourth argument. An exclusive word removes from companionship only what is separate from what it is joined to, and the Son is in the Father (Dist. 9).
claims: The Son is in the Father.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e239.summary: Fifth argument. An exclusive word joined to an antecedent does not exclude its consequent ('only man runs, therefore animal does not run' does not follow), and the Son follows on the Father and conversely (Ambrose, Dist. 9).
claims: An exclusive word does not exclude what follows from its term.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e245.summary: Second sed contra. One exponent of 'the Father alone is God' is 'nothing other than the Father is God', which is false, since the Son, who is other than the Father, is God.
claims: 'Nothing other than the Father is God' is false.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e248.summary: Thomas's determination. Some say that in creatures an exclusive word joined to one relative does not exclude the other ('only the father is, therefore the son is not' does not follow), since one relative implies the other. Thomas judges this false. An exclusive word joined to a supposit excludes every other supposit, so since the son is another supposit, 'only the father' excludes him. That one cannot exist without the other does not prevent it, as generation cannot be without alteration and local motion, yet 'only generation is' excludes every other change. Relatives follow one another in being but not in other categories (a father's being musical does not make the son musical), and since 'solus' determines a supposit, it excludes every other supposit, and the mutual implication of relatives does not remove the diversity of supposits. So an exclusive word joined to 'Father' excludes the Son as far as relational opposition goes. But this differs between creatures and God in two ways. In creatures father and son are not one in essence, so the son is another person and another thing; in God he is not another thing. In creatures paternity adds a new, accidental being distinct from the subject's, whereas in God paternity adds no being other than the essence's, which Father and Son share. So in human cases 'only the father' excludes the son in every way. In God, Father and Son are one in essence and distinguished by relations that add nothing really to the essence, so the Son can be called 'another' (alius) but not 'another thing' (aliud). So 'only the Father' can be understood to exclude 'another' (masculine), which excludes the Son and is more proper given the words' consignification, or 'another thing' (neuter), which does not exclude the Son, since the divine essence in the Son is the whole of what the Father is, not a part. 'The Father alone is God' is then distinguished in three senses: false if 'alone' implies solitude; true if it excludes others from the subject's form ('he who is Father, other than whom no one is Father, is God'); and, if it excludes from the predicate, false if it excludes 'another' (masculine), as Augustine first denies it, and true if it excludes 'another thing', which does not exclude the Son, and so it can be granted as in the cited words of Augustine.
claims: An exclusive word joined to a supposit excludes every other supposit, even a correlative.
In God 'solus pater' excludes the Son as alius but not as aliud.
'The Father alone is God' is false in the masculine sense and true in the neuter sense or by exclusion from the subject's form.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e251.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'The Son alone is most high' is to be distinguished like the first, true in one sense and false in another. Also, 'you alone are the Most High, Jesus Christ' is to be understood with what follows, 'with the Holy Spirit in the glory of God the Father', and it is absolutely true that the Son alone with the Father and the Spirit is most high.
claims: 'Tu solus altissimus' is to be read with 'cum sancto spiritu in gloria Dei patris'.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e261.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'God alone is Father', as to the exponent 'God is Father', converts simply into 'the Father is God'. The other exponent, 'nothing other than God is Father', also converts simply, but its converse is not 'nothing other than the Father is God', since subject and predicate are not the same, but rather 'the Father is not other than God', which is true in a way. From this it does not follow that the Father alone is God.
claims: The negative exponent's converse is 'the Father is not other than God', not 'nothing other than the Father is God'.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e264.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Only the Father' excludes the Son if 'alone' means 'not with another' in the masculine, but not if in the neuter, and this is how Augustine's statement is understood, as his 'because these three are one' shows.
claims: Augustine means exclusion in the neuter sense, which does not exclude the Son.

ta-l1d21q1-d1e267.summary: Reply to the arguments about part, consequent, and mutual indwelling. They do not follow, since a part is not another supposit from the whole but is included in the whole's supposit, and 'animal' as consequent is not a different supposit from 'man'. Although the Father is in the Son by unity of essence and by the understanding of relation, relation, as having the character of opposition, distinguishes Father from Son in supposit.
claims: Relational opposition distinguishes supposits despite mutual indwelling.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e143.summary: Sub-question 1 states arguments that 'God alone is God' is false, from solus as adjective implying solitude, descent to the persons, and God's being with creatures, against the propriety of divinity to God.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e164.summary: Sub-question 2 asks whether 'God alone is Father' is true, given that paternity is also in creatures, against the transfer of exclusive predication from common to proper.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e176.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 1 distinguishes categorematic 'solus' (solitary), which cannot be said of God, from syncategorematic 'solus', which excludes others from the subject's form or from the predicate, in which senses 'God alone creates' is true. Exclusive words immobilize their term, so descent is valid only under the affirmative exponent, and God is alone in his proper nature and operation.
claims: Categorematic 'solus' is false of God; syncategorematic 'solus' can be true.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e199.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 2 holds that 'God alone is Father' is true by exclusion from the subject's form or of the subsistent person, and false of paternity taken formally and univocally, though paternity is said of God and creatures analogically.
claims: 'God alone is Father' is true in some senses, given the analogy of paternity.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 21 introduces Lombard's inquiry into exclusive words ('solus', 'tantum') joined to divine names, on the side of the subject and of the predicate, and announces the corresponding articles.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e135.summary: Article 1 asks whether an exclusive word can be added on the side of the subject to an essential term. Thomas distinguishes categorematic 'solus', which implies solitude and is false of God, from syncategorematic 'solus', which excludes others either from the subject's form or from sharing the predicate. 'God alone is God' and 'God alone creates' are true in these senses. Descent from the exclusive proposition is valid only under its affirmative exponent, and 'God alone is Father' is true in some senses, paternity being analogical.
claims: Exclusive words with essential subjects are true in their syncategorematic senses.

ta-l1d21q1-Dd1e212.summary: Article 2 asks whether an exclusive word can be added to a personal term with an essential predicate ('the Father alone is God'). Rejecting the view that an exclusive word joined to one relative does not exclude its correlative, Thomas holds that it excludes every other supposit. But since in God the Son is 'alius' and not 'aliud' from the Father, 'only the Father' excludes the Son in the masculine sense and not in the neuter. So 'the Father alone is God' is false in the masculine sense and true in the neuter sense or by exclusion from the subject's form, which is how Augustine's dicta are to be read.
claims: 'The Father alone is God' is false if 'solus' excludes another person, true if it excludes another thing.
Relational opposition distinguishes supposits despite mutual indwelling.

ta-l1d21q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 21 examines the logic of exclusive words ('solus') joined to divine subject terms. Article 1 distinguishes categorematic 'solus', implying solitude and inapplicable to God, from syncategorematic 'solus', which excludes others from the subject's form or from the predicate. In these latter senses 'God alone is God', 'God alone creates', and, given the analogy of paternity, 'God alone is Father' are true, with descent valid only under the affirmative exponent. Article 2 holds that an exclusive word joined to a supposit excludes every other supposit, even a correlative. In God, however, the Son is another person but not another thing, so 'the Father alone is God' is false if it excludes another person and true if it excludes another thing.
claims: Categorematic 'solus' cannot be said of God; syncategorematic 'solus' can.
'The Father alone is God' is false in the masculine sense and true in the neuter sense.
An exclusive word excludes every other supposit, including correlatives.
